nameStory: Scapholeberis gets its name from Greek words meaning 'boat' and 'shoulder,' referring to the distinctive boat-like shape of its shell when viewed from the side. The species was named after researcher Rammner, though little is known about this particular scientist. Water fleas like this one earned their common name because they seem to 'hop' through the water in short bursts, much like fleas jumping.
description: Scapholeberis rammneri is a tiny water flea, a type of microscopic crustacean that lives in freshwater ponds and lakes. These translucent creatures are barely visible to the naked eye, measuring less than 2 millimeters long. They have a distinctive boat-shaped shell (called a carapace) that protects their body, and they swim using large, branched antennae that work like tiny oars. Like other water fleas, they filter microscopic algae and bacteria from the water for food.

idTips.label: Boat-shaped shell
idTips.description: The clear, translucent shell curves in a distinctive boat-like profile when viewed from the side, more pronounced than other water fleas

idTips.label: Swimming motion
idTips.description: Moves through water in jerky, hopping motions using large, feathery antennae as paddles

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small at 1-2mm long, just barely visible as tiny moving specks in water samples

idTips.label: Transparency
idTips.description: Body is nearly completely transparent, allowing you to see internal organs and developing eggs

idTips.label: Surface preference
idTips.description: Often found near the water surface among floating vegetation or debris

habitat: Found in shallow, vegetated areas of freshwater ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. They prefer areas with abundant aquatic plants and organic matter where microscopic algae and bacteria thrive. Look for them in the top few inches of water, especially near emergent vegetation like cattails or submerged plants.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to grow as water warms and algae blooms provide abundant food. Best time to find them as numbers increase rapidly.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance during warm months when algae and bacteria are most plentiful. Most active during cooler parts of the day.
seasonality.fall: Numbers decline as water cools, but still present in protected, warmer areas of water bodies.
seasonality.winter: Survive as dormant eggs in sediment, virtually impossible to observe during ice-covered months.

funFact: Water fleas like Scapholeberis can reproduce without mating through a process called parthenogenesis, essentially creating genetic clones of themselves - meaning a single female can start an entire population in a new pond!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other water fleas in the genus Daphnia, but Scapholeberis has a more distinctly boat-shaped profile. Memory trick: 'Scapho' sounds like 'schooner' - both are boat-shaped and travel through water.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'fleas,' water fleas are actually more closely related to lobsters and crabs than to insects. The name comes purely from their hopping swimming style, not from any actual relationship to the biting fleas that bother pets.
compareHints: **Note: Information about this rare species is limited - only one observation recorded in New England.** Compared to the more common Daphnia water fleas found in the same family, Scapholeberis has a more pronounced boat-like shell shape and tends to stay closer to the water surface. Unlike Daphnia, which often migrate vertically in the water column, Scapholeberis typically remains near aquatic vegetation.
